routes.title: Admissible pairs, p-adic Hodge structures and the bi-analytic Ax–Lindemann theorem
routes.brief:
Design a roadmap for Howe–Klevdal's theory of admissible pairs and p-adic Hodge structures in families, ending with the bi-analytic Ax–Lindemann theorem (arXiv:2308.11064; Invent. Math. 244 (2026) 455–530). Its final theorems, stated exactly as in the paper (arXiv v2 numbering):

Theorem 9.1.3 (bi-analytic Ax–Lindemann). Let G/Q_p be a connected linear algebraic group, [μ] a conjugacy class of cocharacters of G_{Q̄_p} admitting a basic class [b] ∈ B(G, [μ^{-1}]), b ∈ [b], M = M_{b,[μ]}, L/Q̆_p([μ]) a p-adic field and C = L̄^. (1) Hodge (resp. Hodge–Tate) special subvarieties are Hodge (resp. Hodge–Tate) Zariski closed irreducible Hodge (resp. Hodge–Tate) analytic sets in M_C. (2) The Hodge–Tate (resp. Hodge) analytic Zariski closure of an irreducible Hodge (resp. Hodge–Tate) analytic set is a Hodge–Tate (resp. Hodge) special subvariety unless the defining intersection is indexed by the empty set. In particular, special subvarieties are the only closed bi-analytic sets in M_C. Theorem A is the minuscule case.

Theorem B. Let Z be a geometrically irreducible rigid analytic variety over a strict p-adic field L and A = (W, L_ét) a neutral admissible pair on Z^♢. Then A has a generic motivic Galois group G and is good with lattice invariant [μ] defined over L; for C = L̄^ and Z̃ → Z_C^♢ a geometric connected component of the associated G(Q_p)-torsor, π_HT(Z̃) is rigid Zariski dense in any connected open of Fl^♢_{[μ],L([μ])} that it meets.

Also export: Theorem 3.2.1 and Theorem 3.3.1 (lattices versus filtrations over diamonds and smooth rigid spaces); Theorem 4.2.2 (basic strata of Bun_G for non-reductive G); Theorem 5.0.4, Lemma 5.1.1 and Proposition 5.2.1 (the B_dR^+-affine Grassmannian of a connected linear algebraic group); Theorem 7.1.2, Theorem 7.2.3 and Propositions 7.3.3, 7.3.4 and 7.5.2 (neutral admissible pairs, types over rigid bases, admissible loci and their special subdiamonds); Theorem 8.5.1 (basic duality); Proposition 9.3.4 and Lemma 9.3.1 (the Hodge generic locus).

Coverage, in order. (0) Part I (Howe–Klevdal, 'Admissible pairs and p-adic Hodge structures I: transcendence of the de Rham lattice', arXiv:2308.11065, Algebra Number Theory 20 (2026) 971–1028) first, as the foundation, the way Pan's first paper precedes his second in DESIGN-PAN: admissible pairs and p-adic Hodge structures over C and their Tannakian properties (Theorems 4.3.5, 5.1.6), lattices, filtrations and goodness (Theorem 3.2.6), the specialization theorem 3.5.1, Proposition 3.1.7, invariants and B(G, [μ^{-1}]) for non-reductive G (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.4.4), existence (Example 5.4.6), Galois representations (Theorem 5.5.1, Corollary 5.5.3) and Corollary C. Part I's transcendence theorems that Part II does not use may be scheduled with it. (1) Relative foundations: rigid analytic diamonds, Λ-local systems, G(B)-local systems, the Zariski closedness lemma 2.3.2, latticed and bilatticed local systems, trace filtrations, types, Theorem 3.2.1 and Theorem 3.3.1. (2) G-isocrystals, basic classes, G_b and Bun_G for connected linear algebraic G, Theorem 4.2.2, twisting (Lemma 4.2.3). (3) The B_dR^+-affine Grassmannian, Schubert cells and the Bialynicki-Birula map for connected linear algebraic G (Section 5). (4) Neutral p-adic Hodge structures, X_[μ], Hodge–Tate loci and special subvarieties (Section 6). (5) Neutral admissible pairs: Tannakian structure, realizations, G-structure and motivic Galois groups, types over rigid bases, b-admissible loci, Hodge loci, functoriality, special subdiamonds and subvarieties, and Examples 7.5.7–7.5.10 (Section 7). (6) Infinite level: M_b, its modification description, period maps, torsor structures, the three notions of special subvariety and basic duality (Section 8). (7) The Hodge generic locus (Definition 9.3.2 to Lemma 9.3.5, Lemma 9.3.1), the submersion argument and Theorems 9.1.3, A and B. (8) Applications (Section 10): variations of p-adic Hodge structure, the cover S̃^cris and the map (10.1.1.1), the Katz–Igusa example, basic loci of Hodge-type Shimura varieties (conditional on the basic uniformization of Daniels–van Hoften–Kim–Zhang, not yet planned), and products of Shimura curves.

Non-reductive extensions. Layers (2)–(3) prove the non-reductive statements from the reductive ones by the Levi decomposition and the unipotent radical; they must import, not repeat, the reductive theory: Bun_G, uniformization and basic strata (BunGAndNewtonStrata BG0, BG1, BG2:uniformization, BG3), Beilinson–Drinfeld Grassmannians, Schubert cells and their smoothness (GeometricSatakeAndFusion GS0:loop-geometry, GS0:Schubert-smoothness), and modifications (RelativeFarguesFontaine RF4).

Imports. DiamondsAndVStacks D1, D2, D4, D5, D6 (diamonds, locally closed subdiamonds, diamondification, and the seminormal full faithfulness this paper adds to D6); FarguesFontaineDiamonds and RelativeFarguesFontaine RF2:untilts, RF4 (B_dR^+, B_dR, modifications); VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals VB0, VB1, VB2:ampleness, VB4 (isocrystals, bundles, slope-zero bundles as local systems); PadicHodgeTheory P8 (OB_dR and Scholze's functor M, which this paper adds to P8) and R06.2; HodgeTateAndCanonicalSubgroups T6:comparison (Liu–Zhu rigidity); HeckeStacksAndLocalShtukas HS2 (local shtuka moduli for reductive G, with the Rapoport–Viehmann and Gleason–Lourenço inputs this paper adds there); DiamondSixOperations S3–S4 (cohomological smoothness, Künneth); PerfectoidQuotients Q4; MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles MC.6 (Tannakian reconstruction); AdicSpacesPartII R3 and its proposed Part II on rigid-analytic Zariski geometry (resolution, Conrad, Bhatt–Hansen, constant rank); the Tau Ceti Reductive algebraic groups roadmap (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ReductiveGroups) and its proposed Part II on stabilizers, observable subgroups and Levi decompositions; ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.0; EndoscopicTransferAndUnitaryTraceComparison ET.6a and HilbertModularVarietiesAndShimuraCurves R18.5 (Lubin–Tate/Drinfeld towers and Čerednik–Drinfeld uniformization, for the examples); PerfectoidShimuraVarieties S2–S3; Tau Ceti's Tannaka reconstruction (TauCeti.Tannaka.pointsFunctorIsoTensorAutFunctor) and Mathlib's Baire category theorem.

Tests: G_a (Example 5.0.5), tori (Example 7.5.7), the Borel of GL_2 (Remarks 4.1.1, 7.5.3), GL_3 with a parabolic (Example 7.5.10), the mirabolic of Res_{E/Q_p} GL_2 (Example 8.4.4), GL_4 (Example 1.1.4), the height-two Lubin–Tate case and its special points P^1(F) (Remark 7.5.8), the non-basic Serre–Tate counterexample (Remark 9.1.4) and the disc family of Example 3.1.1. Boundary: Part III (arXiv:2603.22610) on non-neutral pairs, variation and unlikely intersection extends this roadmap later; the expectation that S̃^cris is potentially unramified is conjectural and is not a target.

Corrections from the review (REV-PAPER-HOWE-KLEVDAL-26, against arXiv v2), to respect when stating the layers:
- Smoothness: Theorem 3.3.1 is stated for smooth S. Lemmas 6.3.3 and 7.4.4 and the proof of Theorem 7.2.3 (E13) apply it, or Liu–Zhu 3.9, to seminormal or singular S. Route them through Theorem 5.0.4(4), or through a resolution S̃ → S. Liu–Zhu is stated only over finite extensions of Q_p.
- Theorem 3.3.1(3) needs a descent step from the pro-étale trace filtration to a filtration on X_ét (Scholze–Weinstein 10.2.3, the paper's Proposition 5.0.3(4)).
- Families: the paragraph after Example 6.0.2, that HS°(Y) is abelian, needs the family argument (fibrewise semistable bundles are pro-étale locally trivial). Proposition 6.4.1 needs the step that ℓ lies in a single even weight; it is commented out in the TeX.
- Motivic Galois groups: prove that MG(𝒢, y) is connected (§7.5 assumes it). Lemma 7.5.1 needs Y connected. In Proposition 7.5.2, Hdg(ℓ) is the disjoint union over ker(H^1(Q_p, H) → H^1(Q_p, G)) of basic loci, so Gr_H^{b_H-adm} is only an open and closed piece of it (SL_2 ⊃ anisotropic torus). The proposition itself holds.
- Section 9: Lemma 9.3.1 is used for Z only irreducible, so state it that way; its proof works. Lemma 9.3.3 holds only in the forward direction, and for single points. Part I Corollary 5.5.3 needs a strict p-adic field, so pass to the maximal unramified extension of the field of definition. Lemma 9.3.5 needs only an infinite residue field.
- arXiv v1's Lemma 4.1.1 (E14) is false for non-reductive G in general; follow v2's Theorem 4.2.2.
routes.reason: Nothing in the atlas goes in this direction. No layer plans admissible pairs or p-adic Hodge structures as Tannakian categories, their families over diamonds, local Shimura varieties for non-reductive groups, Hodge and Hodge–Tate loci, special subvarieties, or p-adic functional transcendence. HeckeStacksAndLocalShtukas HS2 plans local shtuka moduli of reductive groups for the cohomology of Fargues–Scholze; PadicHodgeTheory plans period rings, Galois representations and comparison theorems; LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory and the Mok–Pila–Tsimerman proposal plan complex, o-minimal functional transcendence. A Part II of any of them would mix directions. The non-reductive extensions of Bun_G and of the B_dR^+-Grassmannian (layers 2–3) are kept here because this programme is their only consumer and they are proved from the reductive owners along the Levi decomposition; see the report's judgement calls. Part I, not yet in the atlas, is covered first as the foundation.

routes.title: Reductive algebraic groups, Part II: stabilizers of lines, observable subgroups and Levi decompositions
routes.brief: Extend the Tau Ceti roadmap Reductive algebraic groups (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ReductiveGroups), starting where it stops: its Layer 3 treats quotients G/H as fppf sheaves and names Matsushima's affineness for reductive H, its Layer 5 the unipotent radical and its Layer 7 the Levi decomposition of parabolic subgroups, but it states neither Chevalley's stabilizer theorem, nor quasi-affineness of observable quotients, nor Mostow's Levi decomposition of an arbitrary connected group. Final theorems, over a field k of characteristic zero (Q_p in the consumer): (1) Levi decomposition (Mostow): a connected linear algebraic group G is M ⋉ U with U its unipotent radical and M reductive, Levi subgroups being U(k̄)-conjugate; consequently conjugacy classes of cocharacters of G and G/U agree. (2) For G connected, Z(G) = ker(Ad: G → GL(Lie G)) (Humphreys, Theorem 13.4). (3) Chevalley: every closed subgroup H ≤ G is the stabilizer of a line in a finite-dimensional representation, and one may use the countable family ∧^j V_i for any exhaustion Q_p[G] = ∪ V_i by finite-dimensional subrepresentations (Borel, proof of Theorem 5.1). (4) Observable subgroups: if H ≤ G is the stabilizer of a vector, G/H is quasi-affine (Thang–Bac, Theorem 9; Grosshans); every connected G is observable in GL_n × G_m via ρ × χ^{-1}. Import Layers 1 (comodules, faithful representations; Tau Ceti's TauCeti.Tannaka reconstruction), 2 (Lie algebra, adjoint action), 3 (quotients) and 5 (unipotent radical). Tests: the Borel of GL_2 (not observable-closed: GL_2/B = P^1 is not quasi-affine), the mirabolic of GL_2 as a stabilizer of a vector, and G_a ⋊ G_m. Consumer: the proposed AdmissiblePairsAndPadicHodgeStructures (Sections 5.1, 6.4, 7.5, 9.3 of Howe–Klevdal II).
routes.reason: These are general facts about linear algebraic groups that the Tau Ceti roadmap does not state (its Levi decomposition is for parabolics; its quotient layer stops at fppf quotients and Matsushima). They belong with that roadmap, not with the p-adic consumer, and a Tau Ceti roadmap is extended by a Part II.

routes.title: Adic Spaces PartII, Part II: rigid-analytic Zariski geometry, classical points and resolution
routes.brief: Extend AdicSpacesPartII (Adic Spaces PartII: analytification, formal models, coherent sheaves, étale sites) with the Zariski-geometric facts about rigid analytic varieties over non-archimedean fields of characteristic zero that Howe–Klevdal II uses and the atlas does not plan, starting where R3 stops (coherent ideals, Kiehl finiteness). Final theorems: (1) classical points: rigid analytic points of Y^♢ correspond to classical points of Y, which are dense (Remark 2.2.2 of Howe–Klevdal II); (2) Conrad, Irreducible components of rigid spaces, Lemma 2.1.4: a Zariski closed subset of an irreducible rigid space other than the whole is nowhere dense; (3) Bhatt–Hansen, The six functors for Zariski-constructible sheaves in rigid geometry: weakly Shilov points (Definition 2.4) are dense and lie in no nowhere dense Zariski closed subset (Corollary 2.10); (4) Temkin's functorial resolution of singularities for rigid analytic varieties in characteristic zero (Duke Math. J. 161 (2012), Theorem 5.3.2 as cited), obtained from functorial desingularization of quasi-excellent schemes and gluing — importing the algebraic resolution of AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.7, whose stated scope is varieties only; (5) stratification of a reduced rigid variety into finitely many smooth Zariski-locally closed subvarieties and density of the maximal-rank locus of df; (6) classical points of smooth rigid varieties as p-adic analytic manifolds, and Serre's constant rank (subimmersion) theorem for analytic maps (Lie algebras and Lie groups, Part II, Chapter III), with the submersivity of orbit maps; Mathlib's manifolds over complete fields and its inverse and implicit function theorems (ImplicitFunctionData) are the starting point; (7) Raynaud: over an algebraically closed residue field, a closed set containing the L'-points of a disc contains its Gauss point. Import AdicSpacesPartII R0–R3, the Tau Ceti Foundations of adic spaces roadmap, DiamondsAndVStacks D6. Tests: the closed disc and its Gauss point, a nodal curve and its normalization, and z ↦ z^2 on the disc (rank drop at 0).
routes.reason: General rigid-analytic geometry: classical points, irreducible components, weakly Shilov points, resolution of singularities and constant rank. AdicSpacesPartII owns rigid-analytic foundations (R0–R5) but stops at coherent sheaves; AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.7 limits its resolution to varieties. They are routed to the foundational owner rather than the consumer.

D6 builds the diamond of an analytic adic space and proves the ECD 15.6 comparisons, stating that it does not prove full faithfulness on all analytic adic spaces. Scholze–Weinstein Proposition 10.2.3 (full faithfulness on seminormal rigid varieties, through seminormalization), which this paper uses to define rigid analytic diamonds, is the natural addition to D6.

P8 constructs OB_dR, local acyclicity and the relative Poincaré lemma from Scholze's p-adic Hodge theory for rigid-analytic varieties and applies them to proper smooth comparison. Scholze's functor M from Griffiths-transversal filtered flat bundles to B_dR^+-local systems and de Rham local systems (§§7–8 there), and the comparison of B_dR^+-local systems on the pro-étale site and on the diamond, are the next results of the same source; this paper is a source for them.
BG1 constructs the Kottwitz map, Newton points and their partial order and proves the uniqueness statements for basic classes; Kottwitz's set B(G, [μ]) and its unique basic element belong there.

HS2 defines local shtuka moduli of reductive groups with arbitrary bounds. The non-emptiness criterion (Caraiani–Scholze Proposition 3.5.3, Rapoport–Viehmann Proposition 3.1) and the geometric connectedness of the admissible loci (Gleason–Lourenço) are basic properties of these moduli and their period domains; this paper uses both and extends them to non-reductive groups in its own roadmap.

LD.6 builds Pila–Zannier applications from independent functional-transcendence inputs, and names Ax–Lindemann among them; Klingler–Ullmo–Yafaev's hyperbolic Ax–Lindemann theorem, quoted here for comparison, is such an input. If the Mok–Pila–Tsimerman extraction's proposed Part II (functional transcendence and Ax–Schanuel for Shimura varieties) is accepted, it would own this theorem instead.

M_{b,[μ]} is a diamond over Spd Q̆_p([μ]), while L, a p-adic completion of the reflex field, contains neither Q̆_p nor an algebraically closed residue field. The uniformization of the basic locus is over the completed maximal unramified extension, as §10.2 does explicitly ('the base change of Sh to Q̆_p'), and Theorem A needs such a field. Γ acts on M_{b,[μ]}/K_p, and the component is the quotient, not a product with the discrete set Γ. The discussion is informal and no result depends on it.
